name: Zinc oxide
lead: Zinc oxide (ZnO) is an inorganic white powder used as a mineral UV filter in sunscreens and as a skin protectant in diaper-rash creams, barrier ointments and calamine lotion [1][2]. Wikipedia calls it the broadest-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber among sunscreen filters and states it is completely photostable [1].

Zinc compounds have been used in ointments for a very long time; an Indian medical text, the Charaka Samhita, mentions a zinc salve for eyes and wounds [1]. As of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were recognised as generally recognised as safe and effective (GRASE) sunscreen filters by the US FDA; the EU approved zinc oxide as a UV filter in 2016 [3].
Larger particles produce a white cast, so many modern sunscreens use nanoparticle forms; these are a separate entry on this wiki [1][3][4].

paras: As a sunscreen filter it absorbs UVA (320 to 400 nm) and UVB (280 to 320 nm) [1]. Early-2000s research found it superior to titanium dioxide between 340 and 380 nm [3]. Non-nano mineral sunscreens may leave an opaque white cast that consumers often reject, and people tend to apply them more thinly than chemical sunscreens [3]. Environmental advocates often recommend mineral sunscreens for coral reef protection as a precaution [3].

It is used in products for diaper rash, eczema itch, contact dermatitis and acne, in baby powder, barrier creams, calamine lotion (mixed with about 0.5% iron(III) oxide) and athletic tape [1]. Most industrial zinc oxide goes into rubber manufacturing [1]. Zinc oxide is also an ingredient in dental materials such as zinc oxide-eugenol cements [5].

Its wide band gap of roughly 3.3 to 3.4 eV gives strong UV absorption [1]. Fine particles show antibacterial activity, and proposed mechanisms include reactive oxygen species generation, release of zinc ions and membrane disruption [1][6].

Wikipedia describes zinc oxide as non-toxic, nonirritating, nonallergenic and non-comedogenic, and the FDA lists it as GRAS as a food additive [1]. Inhaling high concentrations of fumes, for example while welding galvanised steel, can cause metal fume fever [1]. Laboratory work shows that nano zinc oxide can be toxic to aquatic organisms, largely through dissolved zinc, and to cells in culture [7][8]. In some sunscreens combining zinc oxide with small-molecule absorbers, UV degraded those absorbers and produced toxicity in zebrafish embryos [1].

Registered trials include a phase 4 trial of zinc oxide ointment for recurrent aphthous stomatitis (NCT07565181, n=100, completed 2025), a study of zinc oxide versus MEBO for pressure injuries (NCT07193849, n=76, recruiting), a terminated diaper-dermatitis study (NCT04101890) and a study of singlet oxygen after UVA exposure of skin (NCT05865431, n=17) [9][10][11][12]. Results were not available in the sources used. Studies of zinc oxide as an oral supplement concern zinc nutrition rather than skin appearance.

Zinc oxide sunscreens are discussed in skincare communities as a mineral option for sensitive or acne-prone skin and for tinted formulations, set against concerns about white cast and thick texture. These reflect general sunscreen discussion rather than claims specific to the compound.

card.summary: Mineral UV filter and skin protectant with broad UVA/UVB coverage; also the base of diaper-rash and barrier creams.
card.note: Non-nano forms leave a white cast; nano forms are covered separately.

quick.overview:
Zinc oxide is a mineral powder used as a sunscreen filter and as a skin protectant in diaper-rash and barrier creams. It covers both UVA and UVB and is described as photostable.

As of 2021 it and titanium dioxide were the only FDA-recognised GRASE sunscreen filters. Larger particles leave a white cast.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UV light because of its wide band gap and also scatters some. In skin products it acts as a physical barrier.
quick.risks: It is generally described as non-irritating and non-comedogenic. Inhaled fumes can cause metal fume fever, and nano forms are studied for effects on aquatic life.
